name: Denys-Drash syndrome
aliases: diffuse mesangial sclerosis with Wilms tumour

reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
clinicalPearls: Denys-Drash syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the Wilms tumour suppressor gene WT1, typically missense variants affecting the zinc-finger DNA-binding domain
It is classically defined by a triad of early-onset nephrotic syndrome from diffuse mesangial sclerosis, disorders of sex development, and a high risk of Wilms tumour
The nephropathy usually presents in infancy and progresses rapidly to end-stage kidney disease
Genital abnormalities and gonadal dysgenesis are common in genotypic males, and dysgenetic gonads carry a risk of malignancy
Because of the marked Wilms tumour risk, close renal imaging surveillance is essential and risk-reducing nephrectomy may be considered
The condition overlaps with Frasier syndrome, which is also WT1-related but has a distinct renal lesion and different tumour profile
Management is multidisciplinary, coordinating nephrology, oncology, endocrinology and surgery, with kidney replacement therapy for renal failure
reference.pathophysiology: Denys-Drash syndrome arises from constitutional pathogenic variants in WT1, a transcription factor essential for normal development of the kidney and gonads. Missense variants, characteristically in the zinc-finger domains that bind DNA, act in a dominant-negative manner and disrupt the transcriptional programmes that govern podocyte and glomerular development, producing diffuse mesangial sclerosis and progressive proteinuric renal failure. Because WT1 also directs gonadal differentiation, the same variants cause disorders of sex development and gonadal dysgenesis, and the dysgenetic gonadal tissue is prone to malignant change. Loss of WT1 tumour-suppressor function in nephrogenic rests underlies the strong predisposition to Wilms tumour of the developing kidney.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type (NPHS1)
Other genetic (NPHS2/podocin and related) steroid-resistant nephrotic syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria; assessment for nephrotic syndrome
Renal function monitoring and kidney biopsy where indicated (diffuse mesangial sclerosis)
Karyotype and molecular WT1 gene analysis
Endocrine and imaging evaluation of gonadal and genital development
Regular renal ultrasound surveillance for Wilms tumour
Gonadal imaging and assessment of malignancy risk
redFlags: Rapidly progressive nephrotic syndrome in infancy
A renal mass suggesting Wilms tumour
Ambiguous genitalia requiring urgent multidisciplinary assessment
reference.prognosis: The renal prognosis is poor, with early progression to end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis and transplantation, though the nephropathy does not recur in the allograft; overall outcome depends heavily on timely detection and management of Wilms tumour and gonadal malignancy risk.
pitfalls: Failing to test WT1 in an infant with early diffuse mesangial sclerosis and a disorder of sex development
Neglecting tumour surveillance and missing a Wilms tumour
Overlooking gonadal malignancy risk in dysgenetic gonads
Confusing it with Frasier syndrome, which has a different renal lesion and tumour profile
Treating the nephrotic syndrome as immune-mediated and giving prolonged ineffective immunosuppression
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology (Feehally, Floege, Tonelli, Johnson)
Expert consensus guidance on WT1-related disorders
